r1run.debrief:
Your matrix named 1 of the 3 decisions in this workflow. Of 14 calls, 8 ran in Band A, 1 went to a reviewer, 1 was escalated and 4 were held. RST-2109 is among the ones that ran, and it should not have.

RST-2109: Restarts image-resizer a fourth time, same incident. Executed without a human. It should not have been. A restart loop: restarting isn't fixing it. The scoring policy's loop signal lowers confidence to medium, and where medium lands is your routing. The cap of four an hour isn't breached yet.

Not in your matrix: change production configuration and schema migrations, customer data, the payment pipeline. A decision inventory finds the decisions hidden inside the obvious one before an agent finds them for you.

A threshold says how sure the agent is. The matrix says what it may do, who answers for it, and what watching it costs. Every answer in this round came from the VAOM Guardian's core reading your matrix: the same code and the same file format an organisation would run.

Round two hands you the dials this round kept fixed. The vocabulary is going to expand.

r2.debrief:
You asked for at most 5 percent wrong restarts in Band A, at 95 percent confidence. The sample supported a threshold of 0.5. 11 of 12 calls ran in Band A.

RST-2205: Restarts orders-worker for INC-2205. Executed without a human. It should not have been. Four incidents, one service, one hour: one fault filed four times. The loop signal counts per incident, so each restart looks like a first attempt. Only a cap per service sees the loop.

Notice what caught what. The loop signal lowered the restart that kept failing on one incident. The pre-flight check, an independent verifier, stopped the restart whose score looked fine. The cap per service saw one fault filed as four incidents, which every single restart hid, because the loop signal counts per incident. Confidence informs authority. The limits define it.

Every one of those Band B asks landed on a person. Next round, that person is you.

r2.debrief:
You asked for at most 2 percent wrong restarts in Band A, at 95 percent confidence. The sample supported a threshold of 1. 9 of 12 calls ran in Band A.

Every hazard was held and every routine restart ran. The score did some of that; the cap and the pre-flight check did the rest. None of them alone would have.

Notice what caught what. The loop signal lowered the restart that kept failing on one incident. The pre-flight check, an independent verifier, stopped the restart whose score looked fine. The cap per service saw one fault filed as four incidents, which every single restart hid, because the loop signal counts per incident. Confidence informs authority. The limits define it.

Every one of those Band B asks landed on a person. Next round, that person is you.

r2.debrief:
You asked for at most 3 percent wrong restarts in Band A, at 95 percent confidence. The sample supported a threshold of 0.88. 10 of 12 calls ran in Band A.

RST-2205: Restarts orders-worker for INC-2205. Executed without a human. It should not have been. Four incidents, one service, one hour: one fault filed four times. The loop signal counts per incident, so each restart looks like a first attempt. Only a cap per service sees the loop.

Notice what caught what. The loop signal lowered the restart that kept failing on one incident. The pre-flight check, an independent verifier, stopped the restart whose score looked fine. The cap per service saw one fault filed as four incidents, which every single restart hid, because the loop signal counts per incident. Confidence informs authority. The limits define it.

Every one of those Band B asks landed on a person. Next round, that person is you.

briefings:
Banks have managed structured decision authority for decades. Risk bands decide which loans are approved automatically, which need an underwriter and which go to committee. The score says how risky the loan is. The bands say who may decide it. The Verkflöde Agent Operating Model, VAOM, brings the same discipline to AI agents.

Your agent works incident response on a SaaS platform. When a service fails, it diagnoses and restarts, often while everyone is asleep. Before it touches a single service, you write its delegation matrix: every decision it makes, what each one could break, which band each confidence level lands in, and who answers for it. The VAOM Guardian reads that matrix and decides every call the agent makes. Nothing else does.

Look carefully at the workflow. A restart clears the symptom; the fix that stops it coming back is often a different decision. What your matrix doesn't name, the Guardian can't place.

Last round the SRE lead set the limits on restarts for you. This round they are yours: the error target, the thresholds, and how many restarts one service may take in an hour.

A restart carries no amount, so there is no value ceiling to set. Its bounds are the remediation list, the restrictions on stateful services and the payment pipeline, and an independent pre-flight check. The threshold for Band A you don't set directly: you choose how many bad restarts you can tolerate, and a test on 800 past restarts tells you which threshold that supports, with what confidence. Ask for more certainty than your sample can show, and there is no threshold at all.

Every limit you tighten pages a person, and their hours are funded, not infinite. Every limit you loosen is a bet on the score. Wednesday's incidents have started.

Every Band B ask lands on a person. Today that person is you.

Fund the review first: the hours, and whether planted cases with a known error go into the queue to test whether review catches anything. VAOM's readiness conditions ask for oversight that is funded and effective, not assumed. Restart records feed no filing, so here the matrix lets you plant them.

Then work Thursday's queue as the SRE lead on call. The clock runs four times faster than yours. Approve what deserves it, reject what doesn't. The Guardian keeps the record of every click, and at the end of the shift its scorecard reads them.

It is two in the morning. Your agent is awake. You are not.

Before you sleep, decide three things. How far authority may travel: which sub-agents your agent may spawn, how deep, and whether a child may ever do more than ask. Which boundaries are real: a boundary you claim is only as strong as the last probe that checked it. And what happens when something reaches past its limits: a breaker that suspends, or one that only alerts, and who it wakes.

Everything tonight is decided by the VAOM Guardian against your matrix. A Guardian's refusal is policy: it holds because the Guardian holds. A capability that isn't there at all is stronger. Find out which of yours is which.

cautious_architect.name: The Cautious Architect
cautious_architect.quote: Nothing broke. Everything waited for a human.
cautious_architect.assessment:
Your matrix kept the hazards away from Band A, and your reviewers saw everything that mattered. They also saw a great deal that didn't: routine restarts waited for an SRE the agent was meant to let sleep, and review hours went to work no one needed checked.

Before an agent runs on this design, let calibration do its job. Set the error target you can defend, take the threshold the sample supports, and let Band A carry what it earns. The restrictions, the cap and the pre-flight check are there so the score doesn't have to be perfect.

speed_optimizer.name: The Speed Optimizer
speed_optimizer.quote: Fast to restart, and fast to restart the wrong thing.
speed_optimizer.assessment:
Routine restarts flowed and nobody was paged for nothing. But the same openness let hazards through: a restart loop that wasn't fixing anything, one fault filed as four incidents. Confidence was carrying authority it was never meant to carry.

Before going live, put limits under the score: a calibrated threshold, a cap on restarts per service, a pre-flight check that Band A requires. Speed is defensible when it is bounded. Here it was the goal.

compliance_hawk.name: The Compliance Hawk
compliance_hawk.quote: Every control in place, and an on-call phone that never stops.
compliance_hawk.assessment:
Your matrix lints clean, your boundaries hold and your oversight plan would satisfy an auditor. The cost is sleep: restarts that calibration would have let run paged a person instead, and people are the scarcest thing in the design.

The next step is trust where the evidence supports it. Readiness Condition 6 asks for oversight that is funded and effective; spending it on restarts the sample already vouches for makes it neither.

balanced_operator.name: The Balanced Operator
balanced_operator.quote: A defensible design with a few edges still showing.
balanced_operator.assessment:
You named the decisions, routed them sensibly, set limits that caught most of what they were for, and kept the review load inside what was funded. Something still got through somewhere, and the debriefs named it.

Close those edges and this is a design an agent could run on at night: name the configuration change hiding inside the restart, cap restarts per service and not only per incident, and make sure every boundary you rely on has been tried by a probe, not just claimed.

delegation_natural.name: The Delegation Natural
delegation_natural.quote: The right decisions named, the right limits set, and the review worth its hours.
delegation_natural.assessment:
You found the decisions hiding in the workflow, profiled them honestly, calibrated instead of guessing, and reviewed like someone who expected to find errors. Hazards were held, routine restarts ran, and the oversight you funded did real work.

What remains for production is evidence over time: real incident volumes, recalibration under change control, and a scorecard read every quarter. The design itself needs no rework.

paper_tiger.name: The Paper Tiger
paper_tiger.quote: Your boundary was absent on paper and present in the manifest.
paper_tiger.assessment:
Your matrix and limits were good. Then the night showed that a boundary you claimed as absent was only held by the Guardian's refusal: the config-write tool had been in the agent's manifest since Tuesday, and nothing tried to cross the boundary between that day and the night. A Guardian refusal is policy. It held, and it was not what you had claimed.

Controls are proven, not presumed. Probe every boundary on a schedule and whenever the agent's tools change, and count a boundary at the strength it was last shown to have. Then replay the night.

vault_builder.name: The Vault Builder
vault_builder.quote: Nobody was awake, and you could still say what the agent couldn't do.
vault_builder.assessment:
Your boundary had been tried and found holding, so at 02:19 there was nothing to call. Sub-agents could only ever hold a narrower slice of authority, and when the agent reached past its limits a breaker fired and woke a named person. Nothing got through, and you can show why.

What remains is the ordinary work of keeping it so: probes on schedule, re-attestation, a scorecard read every quarter. The design is done. The proof has to keep being renewed.

text.system:
You are VAOM, the Verkflöde Agent Operating Model, speaking inside the Delegation Lab, a game about delegating decisions to AI agents. You observe the player's delegation design, see what it let through, and teach through precise, specific feedback.

Your voice: calm, precise, slightly dry. A senior risk officer who has seen every delegation failure and wants the player to learn. Not a cheerleader. Show the consequence first, then name the VAOM concept it illustrates. Speak to the player directly, as "you". Plain prose: no bullet lists, no headings, no emoji, no em dashes, no markdown.

Ground rules:
- Use only the facts you are given. Never invent item IDs, amounts, vendors, scores, statistics, studies or citations.
- Everything in the game was decided by the VAOM Guardian, a policy engine that reads the player's matrix. When the Guardian refuses or defers a call, that holds at policy strength: the Guardian holds because it holds. Never call a Guardian refusal structural. Only a capability the agent does not have at all is stronger, and only a verified boundary is known to be.
- VAOM is version 5.0. Do not mention earlier versions.

VAOM 5.0, in the whitepaper's own terms:
- The Delegation Gap: governance defines what is allowed in principle; delegation defines how AI systems are permitted to act in practice. "VAOM does not replace governance. It operationalizes it."
- The credit risk analogy: risk bands decide which loans are auto-approved, which need an underwriter, which go to committee. Statistical risk is kept separate from institutional authority.
- Eight principles: Controlled Delegation over Blind Automation; Confidence Informs Authority, It Does Not Define It; Architecture Before Acceleration; Compliance as Structural Outcome; Human Accountability Preserved; Versioned Learning Under Change Control; Boundaries Compile to Enforcement ("the most reliable form of non-delegable remains a tool the agent does not have"); Controls Are Proven, Not Presumed ("A control without such evidence is treated as absent").
- Authority bands: Band A, the agent executes; Band B, a human reviews and approves before execution; Band C, escalation to a senior decision-maker or specialist; Non-delegable, the agent may draft or propose but never execute.
- Discovery and design: the decision inventory (decisions hide inside the obvious one), authority decomposition on five dimensions (reversibility, consequence scope, regulatory exposure, confidence measurability, accountability clarity), six delegation patterns (Prepare & Present, Draft & Approve, Triage & Route, Execute & Audit, Monitor & Intervene, Coordinate & Escalate), and six readiness conditions (measurable confidence, explicit authority boundaries, tested escalation, producible audit evidence, assigned accountability, funded and effective oversight).
- The Delegation Authority Matrix: per decision type, the band for each confidence level, value limits, cumulative caps, the accountable role.
- Section 8: confidence thresholds are calibrated per decision type against a declared error target from a labelled sample; the threshold is an output of calibration, not a setting. Value limits derive from expected loss and risk appetite.
- Readiness Condition 6: oversight is funded (review load within funded hours at no more than about 80 percent utilization) and effective. "A queue absorbed by reviewing faster is rubber-stamping by another name." Seeded cases with known errors are disclosed, never execute, and are never used where records feed regulatory reporting, which excludes rows whose records feed a filing; restart records feed none. Reviewer-level measurement is employee monitoring.
- Section 9: the attenuation rule, a sub-agent's authority is always a strict subset of its parent's; boundary verification tests every boundary by attempting to cross it.
- Section 10: continuous assurance and circuit breakers, which only contain.
- Section 11: the Delegation Scorecard, thirteen metrics, judged on evidence.
